title: Deployment and operations
source_deliverable: A versioned model behind a validated prediction service, with monitoring, a canary decision and a rollback.
summary: Put a model where other people can use it: choose a serving pattern, define a stable prediction contract, protect the boundary with validation, monitor the service and the model separately, and release updates with a canary and a rollback plan.
outcomes: Choose between batch and online inference for a decision you have to make.
Write a prediction contract that says what inputs are required and what comes back.
Validate inputs at the boundary and reject bad requests clearly.
Monitor the service and the model separately, and say what each signal means.
Plan a canary release with stop conditions and a rollback that has been rehearsed.
existing_source: app/data/machine_learning_pathway.json, module mle.production-ml, lessons mle.production.01 to mle.production.03

lessons.title: Test your service the way a user would
lessons.goal: Write the tests that prove a prediction service behaves correctly for good inputs, bad inputs and edge cases.

sections.heading: The happy path is not enough
sections.intent: Explain that a service that only works on the example from the documentation is not finished, and list the other cases that matter.

sections.heading: Bad input must fail clearly
sections.intent: Show a request with a missing field, a string where a number belongs, and an extra field, and explain what a good error message contains.

sections.heading: Edge cases are where bugs live
sections.intent: Explain empty inputs, extreme but valid values, and repeated requests, using the churn features as examples.

sections.heading: Write the test before the fix
sections.intent: Explain writing a failing test for each bug you find, and how that keeps the bug from coming back.

lessons.task: Write four tests for the prediction contract of the bundled churn model: a valid request, a request missing a feature, a request with a non-numeric feature, and a request with an unknown extra field. Run them and fix anything they catch.
quiz: Why is testing only the example from the documentation not enough?
What should a prediction service do when a required field is missing?
Why does an extra unknown field sometimes deserve an error?

lessons.title: Choose a prediction serving pattern
lessons.goal: Choose batch or online inference based on the decision's latency, volume, and reliability needs.

sections.heading: Batch and online inference solve different timing needs
sections.intent: Compare scoring a file of rows once a night with scoring one row while someone waits.

sections.heading: Define a stable prediction contract
sections.intent: Explain the request and response shape as a promise, and why changing it later breaks callers.

sections.heading: Protect the application boundary
sections.intent: Explain why validation belongs at the edge and what a good error message tells the caller.

lessons.task: For the bundled churn model, write the prediction contract as you would document it: the request fields, the types, what happens on invalid input, and the response fields.
quiz: When is batch inference the better choice?
Why validate input at the boundary of the service?

lessons.title: Monitor data and model behavior
lessons.goal: Detect service failures, input shifts, and changes in model quality with appropriate signals.

sections.heading: Monitor the service and the model separately
sections.intent: Explain that a healthy service can serve bad predictions, so uptime and latency are not enough.

sections.heading: Drift is a signal to investigate
sections.intent: Explain input drift as the incoming data changing shape, and that drift alone does not prove the model is worse.

sections.heading: Set actions before alerts fire
sections.intent: Explain that every alert needs a written action, and give examples of who does what when a signal moves.

lessons.task: Write a monitoring plan for the bundled churn model with four signals: the service ones and the model ones, and for each one the threshold, the action and the person responsible.
quiz: Why can a service be up and still serve bad predictions?
What does input drift tell you and what does it not tell you?
What must accompany every monitoring alert?

lessons.title: Release with a canary and rollback
lessons.goal: Limit the impact of a model update and restore a known-good version safely.

sections.heading: Treat model promotion as a release
sections.intent: Explain that a new model version is a production change with the same care as a code change.

sections.heading: Use stop and rollback conditions
sections.intent: Explain the canary idea: send a small share of traffic to the new version, watch, and stop if a condition is met.

sections.heading: Retraining is a governed decision
sections.intent: Explain that retraining on new data needs the same checks as any other release, and that data drift alone is not a reason to retrain.

lessons.task: Write a canary plan for a new version of the bundled churn model: the traffic share, the signals you watch, the number that stops the release, and the exact rollback steps.
quiz: What is a canary release and why is it called that?
What has to be written down before a release can be stopped automatically?
Why is data drift on its own not a reason to retrain?

project.brief: Serve and operate a model. Package the versioned churn model behind a validated prediction service, run a batch and an online prediction, demonstrate monitoring with a drift signal, and make a canary decision with a rollback that you have rehearsed.
deliverables: A public GitHub repository with a README that states the prediction contract and the operational plan.
A service that validates its input and refuses bad requests with a clear message.
A monitoring demonstration with one drift signal triggered on purpose.
A test file that passes in CI on every push.

rubric.criterion: The prediction contract is stable, validated and tested
Monitoring covers the service and the model with written actions
The canary and rollback decision is explicit and rehearsed
